scenes.text: One article, eighteen questions about it. Why does a chat engine end up reading the article over and over?
scenes.say: One article, and eighteen questions about it. Why does a serving engine end up reading that article over and over?

scenes.headline: How Flide answers every question in one pass
scenes.sub: One shared state, many questions, one flat stream
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Pavlo! Flide is an inference engine for decision models. Let's see how it shares one state with every question, exactly.

scenes.title: What a decision request costs
scenes.sub: A state, a handful of questions, a probability per option
scenes.say: Chapter one. What a decision request costs.

scenes.title: A full QuALITY article, in tokens

steps.term: Decision model: scores options, writes nothing
steps.say: A decision model never writes a sentence. It reads a state, here an article of about five thousand eight hundred tokens.
Then it scores the options for each question. These articles carry about eighteen questions each.
Run each question as its own prompt, and the article is computed every time: over a hundred and seven thousand tokens.
Compute the state once and branch the questions off it, and it's under seventy-five hundred. Fourteen times less work.

scenes.title: Why a prefix cache falls short
scenes.say: Chapter two. Why a prefix cache falls short.

scenes.title: Two kinds of layer in Qwen3.5

left.title: Attention, 6 layers
items: Keeps a key row per token
Any prefix is its first rows
left.say: Engines like vLLM already cache a shared prefix. For attention that is nearly free: a prefix is just the first rows of the cache.

right.title: Gated DeltaNet, 18 layers
items: Folds every token into one matrix
Cannot be cut back to a position
Resume only from a saved snapshot
right.say: But most of Qwen three point five's layers are Gated DeltaNet. Each folds every token into one matrix. You can only resume from a snapshot, and engines take those at block boundaries.

scenes.title: Tokens computed, one QuALITY request
scenes.say: So each question recomputes a tail. On one article, vLLM computes about one point seven times Flide's tokens, and SGLang about four times.

scenes.title: One stream, forked
scenes.sub: Keep the tree as metadata, lay the tokens flat

scenes.text: Lay every state and every question out as one flat stream, and fork the state so each question sees only its state and itself.
scenes.say: Here's the idea. Lay every state and question out as one flat stream. Then fork the state, so each question sees only its own state and itself.

steps.say: The paper draws a request as a tree. The state is the trunk, and each question is a branch.
On the GPU, the tree becomes one flat stream: all the states first, then all the questions.

params.stream: the stream: 15 tokens; three standalone prompts: 27
params.rowsLabel: rows: queries in stream order · columns: keys
legend: Six state tokens, then questions of 3, 2 and 4 tokens
Each question reads the whole state, then its own branch
The same rows as the question asked alone

steps.say: Here is the article's example. Six state tokens, then three questions of three, two and four tokens, all in one flat stream.

steps.term: Fork mask: trunk plus own branch, nothing else
steps.say: The state rows are ordinary causal attention: each token reads the ones before it.
Each question row reads the whole state, then its own branch up to itself. Its siblings stay dark.
Set one question's rows beside the same question asked alone. Cell for cell, they match. Fifteen tokens instead of twenty-seven.

scenes.title: Gated DeltaNet runs in two calls

steps.say: A mask can't separate questions in a recurrent layer. If question two follows question one, it inherits question one through the state.
So Flide runs each such layer twice. Call one reads every state and keeps each request's final snapshot.
Call two runs every question at once, each restarting from its own request's snapshot. In the decoder that is one argument: an initial state per branch, picked by index. Nothing is copied.
The head reads each question's last token and scores its options.

scenes.title: Answers flipped, a 397-question toy
scenes.say: The article checked this on a small NumPy hybrid. The fork matched every answer asked alone bit for bit. Masking alone, or a delimiter per question, flipped answers. Neither half works without the other.

scenes.title: Where 9.5x comes from
scenes.sub: One cell of one table, and the rest of its row
scenes.say: Chapter four. Where nine point five times comes from.

scenes.credit: the launch animation, from a post on X

steps.say: The launch animation tells it. One article becomes eighteen prompts, each repeating the article.
Flide computes it once and forks it eighteen ways. Thirty-seven point seven milliseconds, against about three hundred and sixty for vLLM and SGLang.

scenes.title: Same workload, Flide's lead by model size
scenes.note: from the paper's Table 3, one client
scenes.say: But that is one cell: the smallest model. Move along the row and the lead shrinks. At twenty-seven billion it is one point five, close to the token ratio. At small sizes, most of the gap is per-question front-end work.

steps.say: Where forking really pays is many questions per state. As questions grow, the baselines climb roughly linearly, and Flide adds only each branch's tokens. At sixty-four questions it is twelve point seven times faster.
And for an agent whose history grows, Flide checkpoints the state and computes only the new tokens.

scenes.title: What exact does not mean
scenes.say: Exact has a precise meaning here.

items.text: Equal to the question asked alone
items.say: It means each answer equals the question asked alone, at the same precision.
It does not mean equal to a float32 pass. In sixteen-bit floats, Flide still flips up to two point three percent.

items.text: Bits move with load by default
items.say: And by default, bits move with server load. A batch-invariant flag pins them, at some latency.

scenes.text: Keep the tree as metadata and run one stream: the state is computed once, and every answer stays its own.
scenes.say: Keep the tree as metadata and run one stream. The state is computed once, and every answer stays its own.

recap: Mask attention to state plus self
Fork the recurrent state by index
Biggest gains: small models, many questions
scenes.say: Mask attention. Fork the recurrent state. And expect the biggest gains on small models with many questions. Thanks for watching!
